name: Event-Driven Architecture
intent: Let services react to facts that other services publish instead of calling each other, and understand what that buys (independence, absorbing outages) and what it hides (the flow, the consumers, the order of events).
scenario: Placing an order touches Payments, Inventory, Shipping, Notify and Analytics. Built with direct calls, the order service calls each in turn, a checkout waits for 10 messages, and when Payments is down for 4 ticks at 2 orders per tick, 8 orders fail. Rebuilt with events, Orders publishes OrderPlaced and each service reacts; the customer is answered after 1 hop and the same outage loses no orders, but the flow is now written in 6 places and nobody can say who consumes OrderPlaced from the publisher's code. A later version emits an event for every state change, and one order now produces 23 messages.
problem: A call says to another service "do this", and the caller knows who it is calling and waits for the answer. An event says "this happened", the publisher does not know or care who listens, and the answer is not awaited. That gives independence in time (a consumer that is down catches up later) and in knowledge (a new consumer subscribes without editing the publisher). It also moves the flow out of any one place: to understand what happens when an order is placed, you follow subscriptions through several services, and the consumers of an event may include ones nobody remembers. Orchestration keeps the flow in one workflow service that sends commands and waits, which is easier to read and change but is a central dependency. Choreography has services react to each other's events, which is loosely coupled but harder to see. Practitioners disagree about which to prefer: many use events between teams and a workflow inside one process that has real sequence and failure rules. And events can be overused: an event for every field change is not decoupling, it is a flood.

howItWorks.title: Tell events from commands
howItWorks.text: A command asks one named receiver to do something and can be refused. An event states a fact that already happened (OrderPlaced), is named in the past tense, and has any number of subscribers, including none. If you find yourself writing an event that only one service is meant to handle, and whose publisher expects something to happen, it is a command in disguise.

howItWorks.title: Publish through a broker
howItWorks.text: The publisher writes the event to a broker (a log or a queue with subscriptions) and carries on. Each subscriber has its own position and reads at its own pace. If a subscriber is down, events wait for it, and the publisher is not affected. The price is that delivery is usually at least once, and order is guaranteed only within a partition, so handlers have to cope with duplicates.

howItWorks.title: Choose choreography or orchestration for the flow
howItWorks.text: In choreography each service reacts to events and publishes its own, so the order flow is spread over the handlers of five services. In orchestration a workflow service owns the sequence: it sends a command, waits for the reply, and decides the next step and what to undo on failure. Choreography needs less central code. Orchestration makes the sequence visible in one place, and it is the usual choice for a business process with compensation steps.

howItWorks.title: Make the hidden coupling visible
howItWorks.text: An event is a public contract, and every subscriber depends on its fields and meaning, even though the publisher's code does not list them. Keep a catalogue of events and who consumes them, version the payloads, and trace an order across services with a correlation id. Without these, a field change or a new step surprises a consumer nobody knew about.

howItWorks.title: Handle outages by design, not by accident
howItWorks.text: With direct calls a service that is down fails the callers. With events the backlog grows while it is down and drains after: nothing is lost, but orders finish late and the queue must be sized for the outage. Watch the queue depth and the age of the oldest event, and decide what is acceptable to delay and what must be answered at once.

pros: A slow or down consumer does not fail the publisher, and its backlog is processed after it recovers
A new consumer (analytics, audit, a new feature) subscribes without editing the publisher
The customer can be answered after accepting the order, without waiting for every step
Services can be built and deployed by different teams against a published event contract
cons: No single place shows the whole flow, so reading and debugging it means following events across services
The publisher cannot list its consumers, so a change to an event can break a service nobody remembers
Delivery is usually at least once and unordered across partitions, so every handler must cope with duplicates
Results arrive later, which means eventual consistency and a screen that must show "pending"
whenToUse: Several services need to react to the same fact, and the publisher should not know or wait for them
A downstream outage must not fail the user-facing request, and delayed processing is acceptable
Teams or systems are independent enough that a published contract is a better link than a call
whenNotToUse: The caller needs the result now, to answer the user, so the flow is really a request and a reply
A small system with one team, where a function call is simpler and a debugger can follow it
Flows with strict sequencing and compensation that nobody can see if they live in five handlers; use an orchestrator
pitfalls: Commands disguised as events: an event that expects one specific service to act on it, coupling the two while hiding the link
Hidden consumers: Analytics, Notify and others subscribe to OrderPlaced, and a change to it needs a review of 2 or 3 subscribers that the publisher's code does not name
Events for every state change (23 messages for one order), so there is more traffic and more coupling, not less
Event chains that grow into a loop, where service A's event triggers B and B's event triggers A
Assuming order and exactly-once delivery, so a duplicate or a late event charges a customer twice
Letting an outage hide: the queue is silently growing to 21 events and orders are finishing 8 ticks late, and nobody is alerted
No correlation id, so one order cannot be followed across five services when something goes wrong

roles.label: Broker
roles.description: Holds events until each subscriber reads them.

roles.label: Subscribers
roles.description: Payments, Inventory, Shipping, Notify and Analytics, each reacting on its own.

roles.label: Flow owner
roles.description: Whoever decides the sequence: a workflow service or nobody.

roles.label: On call
roles.description: Debugs a flow that is spread across services.

quiz.question: A team writes an event named ProcessPayment that only the Payments service handles, and Orders waits for the result to continue. What is it really?
options: A command in disguise: it asks one receiver to act and expects an outcome, so it couples the two services while hiding the link.
A well-designed event, because it uses a broker.
A saga, because it involves Payments.
A query, because the sender waits for the result.
quiz.explanation: An event announces a past fact to unknown subscribers. A message that names an action, goes to one receiver and is followed by a wait is a command, whatever transport carries it. Calling it an event hides the coupling.

quiz.question: Payments is down for 4 ticks at 2 orders per tick. With direct calls 8 orders fail. What happens with choreographed events and a broker?
options: The same 8 orders fail, because events cannot be retried.
All orders fail, because the broker also stops.
The broker rejects the 8 orders, but accepts later ones.
No order fails, but the queue grows to 8 and orders finish late once Payments recovers.
quiz.explanation: The broker keeps the events while the consumer is down, so the publisher is not affected. The price is a backlog that drains after recovery and a delay for the orders in it, and a queue that has to be sized and watched.

quiz.question: A team adds a required field to OrderPlaced. Why is that riskier with choreography than with direct calls?
options: The publisher's code does not name its consumers, so subscribers that depend on the event may be missed.
Brokers reject messages with new fields.
Direct calls are never affected by a new field.
quiz.explanation: With direct calls the caller names every callee, so a search finds them. An event's subscribers are registered elsewhere, and any of them, including ones from other teams, may depend on its shape. A catalogue of consumers and versioned payloads makes the change safe.
